subject: gnomeTinkerer
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: gnome tinkerer with a backpack of gadgets.
Style: whimsical low-poly mix.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a small gnome tinkerer character, around a meter tall, standing on a round wooden workshop platform with cogs, a toolbox, and a mushroom, with a leather backpack holding brass pipes, a telescope, and gear parts.

Now I'm working out the skeleton hierarchy -- hips as root, spine segments, neck, head, jaw, arms and legs down to hands and toes -- plus beard and hat accessories, using the clockwork kit imports. I'm figuring out precise height proportions, placing the base, feet, ankles, knees, and hips at specific y-coordinates so the gnome stands correctly on the platform.

Defining joint hierarchy...

I'll avoid that ambiguity by defining head/neck orientation using explicit forward/up vectors rather than relying on default roll conventions, and standardize on world-space coordinates for most part placement, using a left/right side convention where +X corresponds to the left side with an "L" suffix. For the torso, I'm considering building it as a loft across stations tied to the spine chain for simplicity.

For limbs I'll sweep each chain for smooth bending, but the torso is trickier since it needs to extend beyond the spine chain's endpoints to reach the crotch and shoulders — I'm weighing whether to bind the loft purely to the spine chain alone to keep things simple and avoid conflicts with the hips joint.

I'll just use the spine chain alone, skipping the hips/spine duplication concern since both joints exist fine at the same spot. For the legs, I'm setting up a limb chain with hip, knee, and ankle joints to compute the joint positions.

For the foot, I need to add a toe joint onto the ankle tip, giving a four-point path (hip, knee, ankle, toe) — computing the toe position as an offset forward and down from the ankle target, then connecting these with a polyline for now, though a sharp corner will show at the ankle unless I smooth it.

I'll leave the toe joint without a special role. For the limb helper, I'm checking that root is a Point and bends point forward for the knee; using leg lengths of .18 each gives .36 total against a hip-to-ankle distance of .32, producing a slight natural bend forward, which works well for the gnome's pose.

For the chunky boots, I'm using capsule shapes from ankle to toe with a flat sole box and a cylinder cuff ring around the lower leg to keep the look bulky, then placing shoulder points for the arms next.

For a relaxed, non-T-pose look, I'm giving the gnome a gentle A-pose: arms angled out and down from the shoulder through elbow to wrist, with short limb lengths fitting the squat body, and bending the elbow slightly backward for a natural rest position.

For the hands, I'll keep it simple: palm plus four digit chains (thumb, index, middle, and a merged ring/pinky), each a short 2-3 point chain with thin finger radius, oriented outward and down from the wrist so the hand reads as open and relaxed.

Building finger chains...

Now moving to the head: a skin-colored sphere base, big round nose, pointy ears, bushy white or ginger beard, bushy eyebrows, and a tall gnome tinkerer hat in reddish-rust with a brass band, plus goggles pushed up on the brim.

I'm positioning the skull as a scaled sphere on the head bone, adding a separate jaw bone with a small hinge for mouth movement, and planning a chin/mouth piece hidden mostly by the beard, along with a leather and brass backpack.

Now I'm figuring out the mouth: beard covers most of it, so I'll just add a tiny dark ellipsoid at the jaw front to suggest a mouth gap, skipping teeth or tongue detail. For eyes, I'm placing them symmetrically on the face and thinking about decaling simple cartoon eye textures (white sclera, brown iris, highlight) onto the skull surface using directional decals.

I'm sketching eyebrows as thick bushy white capsule shapes drooping at the outer edges, a round pink nose sphere with subtle mottled highlights, and pointy leaf-shaped extruded ears positioned at the sides of the head.

Tracing the five outline points to confirm the ear shape closes cleanly without edges crossing each other.

I'm wary about smoothing causing crossed corners near the sharp tip, so I'll skip smoothing for the ears and keep a small bevel that shrinks to fit, since a low-poly look is fine anyway.

For the hat, I'm thinking a lathe won't give the floppy curled tip, so instead I'll sweep a tube along a curved path with tapering radius from the brim up to a thin, bent-back point — like a classic gnome hat — using a lathe disc for the brim and a tapered round-capped sweep for the curling cone above it.

For coloring, I'll paint it red with a subtle darker patch and stitched-seam texture rather than stripes, then add a brass band or leather strap around the base — generating that as a separate ring loop sweep through the hat surface so it reads like a goggles strap wrapping the brim.

For goggles, I'm placing two cylindrical lens barrels at the front pushed up on the hat, connected by a strap loop, with teal glowing lenses for a cute gadget look. At the tip, instead of a bell or propeller I'll go with a tiny glowing lightbulb — a tinkerer's idea lamp perched on top.

For the beard, I'm planning a big tapered cream-white beard hanging from chin to belly, built from layered blade-like extruded shapes to give it a textured, bearded look.

Writing beard geometry code...

Still working through lock geometry...

I'm planning the moustache as curling swirl sweeps under the nose using bezier curves, plus thinking about adding small ginger hair tufts or sideburns under the hat.

For the body, I'm settling on a color palette: mustard or teal tunic, denim blue pants with a patched knee, leather apron, dark brown boots, brass accents, and a tan leather backpack with gadgets. Now I'm setting up the torso loft stations to build the tunic shape.

The tunic should flare over the upper legs with stations extending down from the hip area. For the apron, I'm thinking of using a decal with an SVG shape onto the torso front—pockets, straps, stitching detail, transparent outside the apron outline—rather than building it as separate geometry, which would be simpler and still read well visually.

Then I want a leather belt swept around the hips using a surface loop with a lift offset, plus a brass buckle box on the front. For the backpack straps, I'm routing two catmull-rom paths from the chest over each shoulder to the back, draping them onto the torso surface and sweeping leather geometry along them.

Now I'm shaping the backpack itself: a tapered box body behind the torso, a curved flap-lid slab on top, and front straps with buckles for visible detail.

Then I want to add protruding gadgets — a diagonal brass telescope with glowing lens and banded rings, plus a clockwork gear train mounted on the pack's back face with a couple large gears and a small one for visual interest, positioning them to face outward.

Still defining gear parameters...

I'm checking that the rotation axis convention makes sense and verifying each gear stays within the pack's width bounds, adjusting angle 50 for gear 1 so its outer radius doesn't overhang too much, then moving to position gear 2 similarly.

Gear 2 needs its own placement check — testing angle -110 with 18 teeth overshoots the pack width, so I try 14 teeth instead at angle -105, which still overhangs slightly. I decide to just widen the pack to 0.36 to comfortably fit everything rather than fine-tuning angles further.

Now I'm sketching out the remaining accessories: a brass gauge dial mounted on the pack's upper right flap, a hanging lantern with a glow effect and chain loops on the left side, a coiled blued-steel spring along the pack side, a copper pipe with a small steam funnel and puff spheres on top, and possibly wrenches sticking out for extra detail.

I'm also planning a rolled blueprint scroll tied to the pack, maybe a tiny clockwork mouse or beetle on the base for character, and designing the base itself as a round wooden stump with workbench clutter — cogs, a toolbox, an oil can, a mushroom, and grass tufts, keeping the footprint around 0.4-0.42 radius relative to the gnome's 0.36 pack width.

Writing lathe outline and paint logic...

Now I'm placing small props on the base, like a toolbox with brass corners positioned away from the backpack, a tiny mushroom for whimsy, and a couple of flat-lying gears to add that tinkerer's workshop feel.

Thinking about rigging structure though — props need to attach to a joint, and the nearest one would be a leg joint, which isn't ideal. I should establish a proper joint hierarchy: a root joint at the ground plane, with hips as the first spine joint underneath it, since that's the standard convention for rig roots.

I'm also mapping out texture needs — things like the eye detail, apron decal, gauge face, a blueprint scroll texture, and a hat emblem, making sure the count stays in the 5-12 range while keeping the lowest points grounded and the max height around G+1.3.

Now I'm setting up helper functions and vector utilities to keep the API usage correct as I write out the full implementation.

Finishing the tone function to blend warm/cool shading based on surface normal, then confirming the SDK exports rgb, mix, noise, paint, and other helpers from one shared module. I'm reminding myself that paints don't count against the flat color limit, so I can use them liberally.

Now I'm settling on a paintSize of 2048 for the texture atlas and starting to write the imports for the builder module, clockwork kit, glow kit, and geometry merging utility that I'll need for the scene code.

I decide to skip mergeGeometries since it's not needed, and remind myself to be careful about unused imports since the typecheck is strict. Now I'm setting up the build function with a createBuilder call for the gnome tinkerer, then starting to define the joint hierarchy with a root joint and hips joint positioned relative to a ground constant, working through the direction and parent inheritance rules for each joint.

Building the spine chain next, using a catmull curve through three points to create spine1, spine2, and chest joints, then figuring out that the chest should be accessed via the joints array rather than a nullable tip property. I continue defining the neck, head, and jaw joints, chaining each one's position and aim direction off its parent.

Now I'm working through the head geometry: sizing the skull sphere, positioning the eyes by azimuth and elevation angles, and placing the nose, checking whether the proportions look right relative to the head radius and torso height before continuing to build out the facial features as scaled sphere parts.

For the eyes, I'll add decals on the skull positioned using the hit point's normal direction, keeping the eye placement symmetric across both sides of the face.

For the eye SVG, I'm sketching a sclera ellipse, an iris circle with a brownish-green tone, a smaller pupil, highlight dots, and a thick eyelid arc, all on a transparent background. I'm also checking that `b.surface(skull)` gives a valid target so I can use `around(center).at(az, el)` to get hit points for placement.

Now I'm figuring out the eyebrows — bushy white sweeps made from a few curve points with rounded caps — and working out where they sit relative to the eyes and the hat brim, since the hat needs to rest just above the brow line on the skull's curved surface. I'm computing the elevation angles and the horizontal radius at that height on the skull sphere to get the hat brim ring positioned correctly.

Settling on eye elevation level with the brow slightly above and the nose center below, then calculating the eye size and azimuth angle so each eye sits at the right horizontal offset on the curved face. Now I'm starting to lay out the beard loft stations beginning at the lower cheeks.

Switching to a sweep with an ellipse radius function along a Catmull-Rom path instead, which is safer than box lofting — using rx for sideways spread and ry for front-back depth, following the downward-forward normal rule for the beard path from the chin down to the jaw point.

Writing beard color grain...

Actually simpler: paints can just return another paint based on position, so I can pick between grey and beard grain by vertical threshold instead of resolving manually. I'll make the beard tip gradient toward a ginger/tan tone near the bottom.

For the beard locks, I'm writing a helper that extrudes small blade shapes hanging from the jaw, tapering the thickness from thin at the tip to thicker near the jaw, with a slight bevel for softness.

Still writing lock shape...

Computing the lock's orientation frame...

I'm laying out the lock rows with varying x positions, widths, and lengths, from a wide top row down to a tapered tip lock, with lower rows layered so upper locks hang over them naturally.

For the moustache, I'm sketching two symmetric sweep paths with points curving outward and tapering radii for a natural furry texture, colored white with grain for the bone head.

Checking the z-depth stacking: the nose sits forward with a protruding radius, so I need to shift the moustache lower in y and shallower in z to avoid colliding with the nose's underside geometry.

The beard sweep path starts near the eye line, and I'm worried its rounded cap at the start could bulge upward and overlap the eyes, so I'm considering forcing a flat cap at the start of the tube instead of the default round one.

I'm plotting the beard's path points down the torso, shortening it to end around the belt so it doesn't overlap the tummy's front curve, checking that the beard's depth sits clear of the torso geometry while noting the apron decal might get covered by the beard across the chest.

Right, the beard would hide the apron bib in the center. I'm settling on a compromise where the beard ends higher up near chest level, leaving the apron's lower pockets and tool details visible beneath it, and now I'm working out the texture coordinates for that pocket region on the apron decal.

For the torso shape, I'm reconsidering using a swept path along the spine chain instead of a loft, defining an elliptical belly profile with a radius function and checking how the path endpoints clamp against the chain's bounds.

I'm tapering the torso with radii that narrow toward the waist and widen slightly at the shoulders, adding rounded caps at the top near the neck, and placing small sphere joints at the shoulders to smooth the transition into the arms, all in tunic-teal coloring.

Now I'm settling on a complementary palette: red hat, mustard shirt with horizontal stripes, teal pants, and brown apron/boots/pack, writing a stripe pattern function for the shirt with adjustable size, width, and wobble, then wrapping it in a shading function to add tonal depth to the striped colors.

Skipping the collar, I'm moving to legs: teal sweeps with a knee patch decal, a stubby chain detail, baggy trouser hips, and capsule boots. For arms, I'm sweeping striped sleeve chains that taper to a cream cuff at the wrist, leaving hands bare-skinned.

Rather than a held prop, I'll keep hands empty with fingers relaxed, and instead hang a wrench prop from a belt loop at the right hip, plus a small brass gauge-bracer on the left wrist. Now I'm defining shoulder and elbow joint positions to build out the arm rig.

Continuing the arm chain, I'm adding the wrist joint and using a polyline through shoulder-elbow-wrist so the sweep gets a natural rounded bend at the elbow, naming the joints shoulderL/elbowL/wristL and parenting the chain to the chest. Next I'll sketch out the palm as a simple sphere for the hand geometry.

I'm now designing a hand-building function that takes the wrist joint, position, and direction vector, computing a palm center slightly forward along the arm direction and giving it a flattened sphere shape for the palm, with fingers and thumb to follow.

Still defining finger geometry...

That totals 5 chains per hand, 10 chains overall, with each finger segment chunky enough to add noticeable joint count — still comfortably under budget. For legs, I'm setting hip and ankle targets and working out how to pass bend direction correctly to the limb function, since the spec is ambiguous about whether a single bend vector should be wrapped in a list.

Now I'm building the leg chain as a polyline with hip, knee, and ankle joints parented to the hips, then adding a toe joint off the ankle with an aim vector along the foot direction, and starting to sketch the boot geometry as a capsule around the ankle.

Designing the boot shapes...

I'll taper the radius sweep from hip to ankle, adding hip spheres for the pants bulge, and place a knee patch decal on the left leg only, then double-check the feet sole alignment matches the ground height.

Now I'm working out the hat geometry: defining a tilted cone-shaped sweep path above the head joint, with a wide base ring tapering to a thin point as it curves forward.

Still shaping the brim geometry...

For the hat material, I'm mottling a red base with a darker red for cloth variation, skipping the stitched seam idea, and instead adding a cog-and-star emblem decal projected onto the hat's front surface using a ray cast to find the right placement point.

Now I'm working out the goggles: twin brass-rimmed lens barrels angled upward and outward on the hat brim, with glowing teal lens circles, a connecting bridge rod, and a strap looping around the hat using a surface loop.

For the hat tip, I'm adding a small brass socket and glowing amber glass bulb positioned at the end of the sweep path, oriented using the path's tangent direction so it sits naturally pointing backward and upward.

Still adjusting the hat's curl so the tip droops a bit more realistically, defining the final set of path points and tapering radii from the brim down to a thin curled point.

I'm checking total height stays reasonable for a stylized gnome around 1.2 meters, then setting up the hat as a swept-bone shape with a flat start cap, rounded end cap, and low-poly circular cross-section for that simple geometric look.

Now I'm positioning the ears so they poke out from under the hat brim rather than through it, adjusting their angle and length so they stick out to the sides and slightly upward without clipping the hat geometry.

I'm sizing the ears a bit comically large, then adding a smaller pink inner-ear slab that pokes slightly through the base ear thickness for contrast.

Next I'm shaping the nose as a flattened bulbous sphere positioned on the face, giving it a mottled pink-red tone plus a tiny white highlight sphere on top for shine. Then I'm adding simple flattened pink spheres near the cheeks to act as blush marks.

Now I'm turning to the backpack: positioning it on the gnome's back using a tapered frustum box shape, sized and placed so it sits above the hips without clashing with the boots, and painting it a mottled dark leather tone with a paneled rivet texture for seams.

Adding pack lid and bedroll...

A brass telescope extends diagonally from the pack's side, built from tapering tube segments with rings and a glowing glass end, strapped into place near the hat. On the other side I'm adding a copper pipe stack rising from the pack's top corner for a steam vent.

Steam puffs emerge as a few simple opaque light-gray spheres, since translucency isn't feasible. For the back face, I'm placing a gear train lower-center and a gilt-bezel gauge upper-left, positioning the gear assembly flush against the frustum's back plane so it sits recessed rather than floating.

I'm also adding a hanging lantern on the pack's left side, attached via a hook bracket and chain, with a glass box body, brass cap and base, a carry ring, and a glowing flame inside.

Now I'm placing a telescope with wrench handles on the left side, and arranging the lantern plus a rolled blueprint scroll (a cream cylinder tied diagonally) positioned under the pack on the right.

I'll go with "GIZMO & CO." for the base sign text, and pin a small blueprint sheet texture onto the lower-left of the pack's back plane, where the gear train sits. Now I'm working out the gear train positions on that back panel, placing gear0's center and computing gear1's offset using the pitch radii and a 50° angle to get its x and y coordinates.

I'm also placing the gauge higher up with its own radius and checking it stays within bounds, and I've decided the blueprint shouldn't go on the pack but instead as a flat unrolled sheet lying on the ground near the toolbox base, textured and lit from above.

I'm listing out the texture set needed across the model -- eye, apron, emblem, patch, flame, sign, gauge, blueprint, gear, toolbox label -- confirming I have at least eight distinct textures covered, then starting to define the blueprint's plane geometry and placement on the base.

Now I'm working out the orientation of the blueprint plane and sign board using the up/axis/dir parameters so the texture reads correctly from the viewer's side, then sketching a small wooden sign on a stake near the back-left of the base with a thin textured board facing forward.

I'm checking placement clearances for the base props against the gnome's arms and hands—figuring out coordinates for a toolbox (rotated slightly, right-front), a couple of mushrooms of varying size, and the sign post—making sure none of them overlap the reaching arm or fingers.

Now I'm scattering some small clockwork props around: flat gears clustered near one side with slight offsets, and sketching a little windup mouse or beetle with a brass dome body and a wind-up key on its back.

Still adding details... I'm also considering a tiny oil can with a spout, and grass tufts made from textured cards scattered in a ring around the base rim to soften the edge.

I'm tallying up ten textures total: eye, apron, emblem, patch, flame, sign, gauge, blueprint, toolbox label, and grass with gears layered in. For the base itself, I'm lathing a rounded platform shape with a slightly flared top edge, then painting bark texture on the sides.
